pr_body:
/kind bug

kube-proxy was always deleting stale conntrack entries for stateless protocols, like UDP and SCTP, since TCP clients retries with different source ports and eventually the stale entries timeout.
However, on TCP clients with a low number of source ports, the stale entries can also blackhole connections, so we need to delete them too.

However, we should be careful deleting conntrack entries, since it can break TCP graceful shutdown, i.e. pods are still using the connection despite the endpoint is no longer present in kube-proxy. To avoid that, we delete only conntrack entries with the SYN_SENT status.


Fixes #101607

```release-note
kube-proxy was deleting stale conntrack entries for stateless protocols, like UDP and SCTP. However, on TCP clients with a low number of source ports, the stale entries can also blackhole connections, so we delete them too.
```

issue_context.title: TCP Conntrack entries remain in stale
issue_context.body:
We have a service with type as LoadBalancer. The service external-IP is allocated by a controller and the this IP is known in advance even before the service is deployed. The service external IP is configured on the client machines located outside the Kubernetes cluster and they are trying to reach the service all the time. The adjacent routers are configured to forward the traffic matching the service external-IP towards the worker node statically.

In the beginning the clients are trying to reach to the service external-IP and at this time the Kubernetes cluster do not have the service or the pods up and running. At this time the iptables do not have entry for the service external-IP and this means that the packets will not be handled by the iptables populated by kube-proxy. These TCP SYN packets creates a conntrack entry which will get removed in 120 seconds if no further packets are matching to the tuple

sudo conntrack -L  | grep 30.4.5.22
conntrack v1.4.4 (conntrack-tools): 48 flow entries have been shown.
tcp      6 48 SYN_SENT src=137.64.100.78 dst=30.4.5.22 sport=63302 dport=80 [UNREPLIED] src=30.4.5.22 dst=137.64.100.78 sport=80 dport=63302 mark=0 use=1

In this case the service external IP is 30.4.5.22

The client is having limited (may be 3) TCP source ports due to the way firewalling and clients are configured. This means that clients keep trying to establish TCP session with same source port and causes the conntrack entry to be alive and not cleaned up at all.

When the service and pods are deployed at a later stage, the iptables are correctly updated with the service externalIP (30.4.5.22) rules. Unfortunately due to existing conntrack entry matching the packets destined to 30.4.5.22, the packets do not hit the NAT table. This means that the clients can not talk to the real service and they do not recover. If the conntrack entries are dropped after NAT tables are updated then the TCP sessions are established correctly.

This issue can happen in some cases of node reboots since there are cases where the external traffic arrives to the node before the kube-proxy can setup the NAT entries for the service external IP.

When we checked the kube proxy code we see that there are logic to remove the conntrack entries matching the service IP in case of UDP and SCTP but not for TCP.

Does it make the system robust if we clear the conntrack entry matching the IP that is added to the NAT table so that we do not have undesired behaviour due to stale conntrack entries?

#### Environment:
Kubernetes version is v1.20.4
kube-proxy mode is iptables
comments: /sig network
/area kube-proxy

> When we checked the kube proxy code we see that there are logic to remove the conntrack entries matching the service IP in case of UDP and SCTP but not for TCP.

Just for clarification, UDP and SCTP are stateless and there is no possibility from the client to understand if the server is still present or has left, so clients keeps sending traffic with same (src ip/src port) renewing the conntrack entry.
Kube-proxy "knows" if the UDP/SCTP server has gone or has been replaced with other IP (new endpoints created or changed), so it clears the "stale" conntrack entries in order that the new traffic is not blackholed forever in conntrack..

> These TCP SYN packets creates a conntrack entry which will get removed in 120 seconds if no further packets are matching to the tuple

TCP is stateful, so it can "know" if the server is alive, as you correctly point out, after some predefined time the client retries if is not able to connect, usually with a new source tcp port that means different "new" conntrack entry, so the old one is not renewed and cleared after the conntrack timeout.

> Does it make the system robust if we clear the conntrack entry matching the IP that is added to the NAT table so that we do not have undesired behaviour due to stale conntrack entries?

This seems a very specific scenario, with alternatives out of kube-proxy to fix it, so I don't know if this can be enough to implement a general solution, it will be interesting to hear others opinions.

It is important to mention that externalIPs is something that the project is restricting since the recent CVE-2020-8554 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/97076

This option has been tried and it helps when the client do not sent TCP SYN  in this time window. But what we have seen is that some of the clients were very aggressive and thus the configuration has to be even smaller numbers and eventually depends on the client behaviour. So we were looking at an option that will clear the entry when a matching service is added to iptables.

Quite easily reproducible. Setup;
* Select a loadBalancerIP, `10.0.0.0` in this example
* Set a static route so traffic to that address comes to one node, `vm-002` in this example

From an external machine, constantly try to connect using the same source port;
```
while true; do date; nc -w 1 -p 40000 10.0.0.0 5001; done
```
On the receiving node (`vm-002`);
```
conntrack -L -d 10.0.0.0      # There should be an entry
# Now create a pod and service
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: alpine-deployment
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: alpine
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: alpine
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: alpine
        image: library/alpine:latest
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        command: ["nc", "-lk", "-p", "5001", "-e", "hostname"]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: alpine-hostname
spec:
  selector:
    app: alpine
  ports:
  - port: 5001
    name: hostname
  type: LoadBalancer
EOF
# If needed, assign the loadBalancerIP
assign-lb-ip -svc alpine-hostname -ip 10.0.0.0
```
Now the service is setup and working but the external machine still can't connect because of the stale conntrack entry. Now we delete the conntrack entry on the receiving node and communication starts to work immediately;
```
conntrack -D -d 10.0.0.0
```
I use [assign-lb-ip](https://github.com/Nordix/assign-lb-ip) to set the loadBalancerIP, it may be set automatically in your env.

It can be observed that since the same conntrack entry is used the connection is "sticky", it is not load-balanced between PODs. If you remove the source port setting it will be load-balanced (or if another source address is used).

While this is not a problem for web-applications where the clients are well behaiving and usually have no restricions on the source port, it _is_ a problem if the client is very primitive or is restricted by firewall rules. IMO K8s can, and should, support those clients.

/triage accepted
The behavior is the same for kroxy-mode `iptables` and `ipvs`.

Thanks for the triage!  Any thoughts on best fix, while it is fresh?

I can reproduce the behaviour, however,  trying to "expand" the current logic we have for UDP to TCP, I realised that we will break graceful shutdown.
1. The  pod is deleted (but has a grace period,default 30sec)
2. kube-proxy will see the endpoint removed, it clears the conntrack entries for that endpoint and remove the NAT iptables rules
3. but the pod will be handling connections during the grace period, breaking them ... and the CLOSE handshake

Andrew has a kep to handle it adding a new state to endpoint slices to handle loadbalancers https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-network/1669-graceful-termination-local-external-traffic-policy but I don't think that we can extend this to ALL services, it seems like a big performance impact on the slice controller.

I have another idea, it is very simple, since we know exactly how the stale entries look like: an entry that is always renewed but never replied, for TCP:

```
tcp      6 119 SYN_SENT src=172.18.0.1 dst=10.10.10.10 sport=60000 dport=80 [UNREPLIED] src=10.244.2.3 dst=172.18.0.2 sport=80 dport=45815 mark=0 use=1
```

for UDP

```
udp      17 29 src=172.18.0.1 dst=10.10.10.10 sport=60000 dport=80 [UNREPLIED] src=10.10.10.10 dst=172.18.0.2 sport=80 dport=60000 mark=0 use=1
```
 
we can do a simple reconcile loop that looks for those entries and delete them, I think that we can also reduce the risk of false positives to near 0, we check entries in an interval T, if we have X matches of
- entry on SYN_SENT (tcp) and UNREPLIED
- entry life timer always renewed (we can check against the sysctl value to see the difference)

we delete it.
This also will decouple the logic of the different proxies and simplify it, current code is complex to read

- I think that for UDP we are good, I revisited again current logic and I think that we clean all possible scenarios.
- I think that SCTP is missing some of the UDP cleanups, I have to check 
- IPVS and iptables proxies logic has diverged

- For TCP I think we don't have to delete the conntrack entries for endpoints, since we have to let the pods to terminate gracefully, however, we should do something with the connections that are not finished in the host, we are also sending the packet back through the same interface that is really ugly.
